en: Wild boar bones and Sus scrofa circeus

Over five hundred specimens, some 97 per cent of the animal remains from the village. Geometric morphometrics on teeth and heel bones, published in 2021, showed these boar were an island subspecies descended from animals brought from the northern Levant, and named it Sus scrofa circeus after the goddess who turned Odysseus's crew into pigs. They were 10 to 16 per cent smaller than their mainland ancestors, and the pigs of later Shillourokambos are their domesticated descendants: Cyprus domesticated its own pigs rather than importing them.

en: An early Neolithic village on a low plateau, excavated by Jean Guilaine's French mission from 1992 to 2004. Its early phases had post-built enclosures, deep wells and pens for cattle, with sheep, goat and pig arriving over time; about 300 blades of Anatolian obsidian show sea contact. Its most famous find is the burial of a man with a young cat beside him.
A man over thirty buried with shells, a stone pendant, flints and ochre, and beside him an eight-month-old cat: the oldest evidence of cat taming.

Deep shafts cut into the bedrock, dug from the earliest phase onwards and, with those at Kissonerga-Mylouthkia, among the oldest water wells known anywhere in the world. Cypriot wells span the second half of the ninth millennium to the middle of the seventh. Nothing comparable is known on the Levantine mainland until considerably later, so this looks like an island invention forced by island conditions.

Aurochs-sized cattle ferried across from the mainland and kept in post-built enclosures. Whether they arrived already domesticated or as managed wild animals is argued from morphology on one side and culling patterns on the other. What is certain is that cattle then died out on Cyprus during the eighth millennium and were not seen again for thousands of years, so the first herds could not sustain themselves.

Ninety per cent of the identified fish from Sector 1 are sea bass and large groupers weighing between four and seventeen kilograms. Fish that size are not caught from the beach, and the village sits several kilometres inland.

Rings of white marble, a material not native to the island. Along with the obsidian and the carnelian at Khirokitia they show that the Late Aceramic Neolithic, usually painted as an inward-looking period, was still receiving things from across the sea.
